description: Bilim, teknoloji ve uzay araştırmaları odağında yenilikçi çözümler geliştirmek için NASA Space Apps Challenge kapsamında bir araya geldik. Takımımızla birlikte üretmeye, keşfetmeye ve geleceğe yön verecek fikirler geliştirmeye hazırız!
summary:
Go for Launch is a browser-based educational game in which students design and fly a complete space mission. Players pick one of five missions (an earthquake-watch satellite over Türkiye, a lunar ice hunter, a Mars weather station, an asteroid sample return, a Europa explorer), then make every key decision in six steps: science goal, instruments, orbit, spacecraft, communications, fuel and rocket. Live bars for mass, power, budget, fuel and data react to each choice, and warning lights explain what is wrong and how to fix it.

The Launch button always works: whatever is left out shows its consequence in the flight simulation, and a “Why did this happen?” report explains the outcome with numbers. Every report includes the success probability over 200 virtual flights. Successful missions earn points, badges and ranks.

The game makes the challenge’s trade-offs concrete: adding one instrument changes mass, power, data and cost together. With a bug-hunt mode, nine task cards, a mini lab and a teacher panel, it is classroom-ready. It is a single HTML file that needs no installation or internet.
details:
What it does and how it works
Go for Launch is a browser game in which a space mission is designed and flown from concept to operations. The player picks one of five missions and one of its three science goals, then moves through six steps: Mission, Science, Spacecraft, Comms, Journey, Flight. Every choice shows up at once in the side panel: the spacecraft drawing changes, five resource bars (mass, power, budget, fuel, data) fill, and warning lights state the cause of each problem and how to fix it. The Launch button always works. The simulation plays out launch, cruise, orbit insertion, science and return with random events (solar storms, part failures). After the flight the player gets a “Why did this happen?” report, a four-part score and the success probability of the same design over 200 virtual flights.

Benefits

  • Mistakes are explained, not punished: students read the outcome in numbers, fix the design and fly again.
  • Ready-made classroom material: a bug-hunt mode (deliberately broken designs), nine auto-checked task cards, a mini lab, a glossary and a teacher panel (lesson plan, rubric, answer key, example solutions).
  • No installation, account or internet; one device per team is enough.
  • Available in Turkish and English.

Intended impact
To bring topics students learn separately (force and motion, energy conversion, how light travels, ratio and percentage, probability, units of data) into a single systems decision, and to teach trade-offs, margins and risk through experience. The audience is grades 5–12 and STEM clubs. The earthquake-monitoring mission shows how space technology serves everyday life through a local example.

Tools, languages, software

  • HTML5, CSS and plain JavaScript; Canvas 2D for drawings and animation. No external libraries, no server; a single file.
  • Progress is kept in the browser’s local storage.
  • Physics model: inverse-square law, rocket equation, orbital period, light-time delay; constants from NASA sources.
  • Testing: syntax checks with Node.js, end-to-end runs with Playwright and headless Chromium.
  • AI: the code, texts and translation were produced with the help of Anthropic’s Claude model; the team directed, tested and revised it through feedback.
  • Presentation: Canva. No special hardware was used.

Creativity

  • Students can start from a broken design instead of a blank page.
  • Decision quality and outcome are scored separately; 200 virtual flights show, through probability, that a good decision can still end badly.
  • The link between orbital inclination and latitude is made concrete over Türkiye: a 30° inclined orbit never sees the country.
  • Success is rewarded with points, six ranks, fourteen badges and a “what your mission gave the world” card.

Factors we considered

  • Simplicity: the first version was too complex; after user feedback it was cut down to six steps and success rewards were added.
  • Scientific honesty: every value is labelled real, model or illustrative; the game does not claim to be an engineering tool.
  • Accessibility: it runs offline and on modest hardware.
  • Balance: five example solutions and five flawed designs were tested over hundreds of virtual flights.
  • Limits: the learning outcomes paraphrase the Turkish national curriculum rather than quoting official codes; team play shares one device, with no simultaneous play across devices.
